title: AI and work: the evidence, in five mornings
subtitle: The WDR, two field experiments, one payroll dataset and Ethan Mollick, so you can stop quoting LinkedIn in the team meeting

source.name: five public sources, linked in each lesson

made_with: Written for AI Tuesday from the sources themselves. Every number and quote was checked against the original PDF or page, with the source linked in each lesson.
audience: anyone who gets asked "so is AI going to take the jobs?" at dinner

days.title: The WDR 2026, in one coffee
days.hook: The Bank's own flagship on AI came out on 4 August 2026. Most of us have read the press release. This is the overview.
days.lesson:
The World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence makes one argument: developing countries cannot sit this one out, and they do not need to build frontier models to benefit. Its framework is three verbs. Adopt the tools that already exist. Adapt them to local languages, data and conditions. Advance, when the foundations are there, toward building more at home. The report's favourite phrase is "small AI": cheap tools that put scarce expertise in reach of millions through text messages, voice calls and basic phones, which matter more for development than the trillion-dollar race at the top.

The jobs numbers are smaller than the headlines suggest. In low- and middle-income countries, about 4.5 percent of existing jobs are amenable to automation by generative AI, against 14.2 percent in high-income countries, while 16.2 percent of jobs could be complemented by AI. The sectors most exposed to automation, such as ICT, finance and business services, employ relatively few people in developing countries. The risk the report names is the one that matters for our clients: AI could close a route to middle-class work by threatening call-centre work and entry-level jobs in software, finance and business services.

For governments, the report gives three roles: enabler (build the analog and digital foundations, from electricity to skills), user (buy and scale proven tools in public services) and regulator (start with existing laws and voluntary standards). On dependence, the advice is practical rather than heroic: do not build every layer yourself, buy from many providers and make sure the pieces can be swapped.

Diffusion is the part that surprised the authors. Middle-income countries accounted for half of ChatGPT's global traffic within six months of its launch. Electricity took decades to reach that point.

quote.text: Developing countries should leave it to the rich world to agonize over whether AI will one day doom humanity. Their own question is more immediate: Will they again arrive late to a technological revolution? Or will they use it this time to improve the lives of millions?

question.q: According to the WDR 2026, what share of existing jobs in low- and middle-income countries could generative AI automate?
question.explain: The overview puts it at about 4.5 percent in low- and middle-income countries, compared with 14.2 percent in high-income countries, while 16.2 percent of jobs could be complemented by AI (figure O.6). The exposed sectors employ few people in developing countries, which is why the number is low and why the report worries more about the entry-level route to the middle class than about mass displacement.

days.do: Open the overview and find figure O.6. Then ask your AI: "For [my country], which of the three government roles in the WDR 2026 (enabler, user, regulator) does my project actually support?" Keep the answer for the next CPF conversation.

days.title: The canaries: who is not being hired
days.hook: The most cited labour paper of the AI era was revised in August 2026 with a year more of payroll data. The number moved.
days.lesson:
Canaries in the Coal Mine? by Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen at the Stanford Digital Economy Lab uses administrative payroll data from ADP covering millions of US workers. The first version, in August 2025, found a 13 percent relative decline in employment for 22 to 25 year olds in the occupations most exposed to AI. The August 2026 revision, with data through June 2026, puts the gap at 19 percent, and it has widened steadily since. The WDR 2026 overview cites the 13 percent version, which tells you how fast this literature moves and why a course built from the source beats one built from memory.

Six facts carry the paper. There is no evidence of widespread, economy-wide job displacement. Young workers in AI-exposed occupations are now 19 percent below where they would be had they kept pace with less-exposed peers, and experienced workers show no comparable gap. The gap works through reduced hiring of young people, not through layoffs. It is concentrated where AI is used to substitute for human tasks; where AI complements workers, employment is flat or rising, especially for experienced staff. And the adjustment happens through jobs, not through base pay.

The authors are careful about what this is: early, descriptive indicators, not a verdict. The patterns weaken when you control for education, some trends predate generative AI, and the ADP sample shows them more sharply than national surveys do. That honesty is the part worth copying.

For us the lesson is about where to look. Headcount in a ministry will not move first. The next cohort of hires, and the tasks they are no longer asked to do, will.

quote.text: employment of young workers in AI-exposed occupations stands 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with that of their less-exposed peers, with no comparable gap for experienced workers
quote.where: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine?, revised 12 August 2026, conclusion (the paper's fact 2)

question.q: Through which channel does the paper say the gap for young workers mostly operates?
question.explain: Fact 4 in the paper: the divergence operates primarily through reduced hiring rather than increased separations, and fact 6 adds that adjustment happens through employment, not base compensation. Layoffs make the news; the empty desk that was never filled does not.

days.do: Think of the last three junior hires in your unit, or the ones that did not happen. Write one line on which of their tasks an AI now does. That is your own canary.

days.title: Two field experiments, one jagged line
days.hook: The same Harvard and Wharton team ran a randomized experiment at BCG and then another at Procter and Gamble. Together they explain most of what you have felt using these tools.
days.lesson:
In 2023, Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Ethan Mollick, Karim Lakhani and colleagues ran a preregistered experiment with 758 consultants at Boston Consulting Group (Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, HBS Working Paper 24-013). On 18 realistic tasks inside what AI could do well, consultants with GPT-4 completed 12.2 percent more tasks, finished them 25.1 percent faster and produced work of significantly higher quality. On one task chosen to sit outside that boundary, the AI users were 19 percent less likely to get the right answer. The authors called the boundary the jagged frontier: AI is excellent and terrible at tasks that look equally hard, and you cannot see the line until you test it.

In 2025 the team went to Procter and Gamble with 776 professionals (The Cybernetic Teammate, NBER Working Paper 33641). People worked on real product innovation problems, alone or in pairs, with or without AI. Individuals with AI matched the performance of two-person teams without it. AI also dissolved the silos: without it, R&D people proposed technical solutions and commercial people proposed commercial ones; with it, both produced balanced proposals. And people working with AI reported more positive emotions, which is not a small finding for anyone who has written an aide-memoire alone at 11 pm.

Put the two together. Inside the frontier, one person with AI is a small team. Outside it, the same person is confidently wrong. The skill of this decade is knowing which side of the line a task is on, and the only way to learn is to check the AI's work on tasks where you already know the answer.

quote.text: individuals with AI matched the performance of teams without AI, demonstrating that AI can effectively replicate certain benefits of human collaboration
quote.where: Dell'Acqua et al., The Cybernetic Teammate, NBER Working Paper 33641 (2025), abstract

question.q: In the Procter and Gamble experiment, one person working with AI performed about as well as:
options: Two people working together without AI
Two people working together with AI
Nobody: AI users did worse on every measure
question.explain: The NBER abstract states that individuals with AI matched the performance of teams without AI. Teams with AI did better still, and AI users across the board produced more balanced solutions and reported more positive emotions. The BCG study is the caution: outside the frontier, AI users were 19 percent less likely to be right.

days.do: Pick two tasks on your list today: one you are sure AI does well (a summary, a first draft) and one you are not sure about (a judgment call on a counterpart). Hand only the first to AI. Check the second against your own answer before you believe it.

days.title: What people actually do with AI at work
days.hook: Anthropic publishes what millions of real conversations are about, and asked 9,700 of the people behind them how worried they are.
days.lesson:
The Anthropic Economic Index is a running series of reports on how Claude is used in the economy, based on privacy-preserving samples of real conversations. The June 2026 report, called Cadences, adds two things: continuous daily sampling instead of a seven-day snapshot, and a survey of about 9,700 people linked to their own usage. It is one company's users, so it is a window and not a census, but it is the largest public window there is.

Three findings matter for an office like ours. First, the output of most AI work is ordinary: conversational outputs such as explanations and guidance, and written deliverables such as documents and presentations, each account for about a third of conversations; code is about a sixth. Second, usage follows the workweek. Work queries subside on the weekend, less so in the highest paid occupations, and tax questions surge before filing deadlines. Third, people choose the most capable models when the task is serious: agentic coding sessions run on the top model 54 percent of the time, against 10 percent of ordinary chat.

Then the survey. More than a third of respondents said it was likely or very likely that their responsibilities would change significantly within a year. One in ten rated losing their own job as likely or very likely. And people were far more worried for others than for themselves: over a third put the probability of a junior colleague losing their job in the next year above 60 percent. Read next to yesterday's canaries, that fear is not irrational. It is the hiring channel, felt from the inside.

The practical point: if a third of AI work is documents and a third is explanations, the question for a team is not whether to use it but which model, for which document, with whose data.

quote.text: Respondents were especially worried about job loss for their junior colleagues, with over one third stating that the probability of a junior colleague losing their job in the next year was over 60%.
quote.where: Anthropic Economic Index report: Cadences (June 2026), survey section

question.q: In the June 2026 survey, what share of respondents rated losing their own job in the next year as likely or very likely?
question.explain: The report says 10 percent rated losing their own jobs as likely or very likely. The one-in-three figure is for responsibilities changing significantly, and the 60 percent is the probability more than a third of respondents assigned to a junior colleague losing theirs. People fear for the desk next to them more than for their own.

days.do: Ask the most junior person on your team one question today: "Which part of your work do you think AI will do next year?" Then compare with what you would have guessed.

days.title: Mollick: the rules, and the new book
days.hook: One professor has written the clearest practical advice on all of this, twice, and his second book came out this month.
days.lesson:
Ethan Mollick teaches at Wharton, co-authored both experiments from Morning 3, and writes the newsletter One Useful Thing. His 2024 book Co-Intelligence gave four rules that still hold. Always invite AI to the table: try it on everything, because you cannot know the frontier without testing it. Be the human in the loop: check, decide, take responsibility. Treat AI like a person, but tell it what kind of person it is: give it a role and context. And assume this is the worst AI you will ever use.

His guide of 18 February 2026 marks the shift from chatting to delegating. Three pieces of advice travel well. Pay for a serious model if you use AI seriously, because free tiers are tuned for speed and many of the errors people blame on AI come from them. Pick the advanced, thinking model yourself instead of leaving the app on automatic. And start with real work: upload a document you actually need, give the AI a hard task, push back on what comes back. Agents such as Claude Cowork, Copilot and the Office add-ins are now where office work happens, and the job becomes managing an AI that does things rather than prompting one that talks.

The new book, Co-Existence (Portfolio, 20 October 2026), is about working with AI that is sometimes, but not always, better than you, which is the jagged frontier from Morning 3 turned into a way of living with it. The honest summary of this whole course is one sentence from him: the technology is uneven, the effects are early, and the people who do best are the ones who keep checking.

If your field is education, there is a sibling to this course: EvidencIA Papers, fifty studies on AI and learning, one a day, same format.

quote.text: I have written eight of these guides since ChatGPT came out, but this version represents a very large break with the past, because what it means to "use AI" has changed dramatically.
quote.where: Ethan Mollick, A Guide to Which AI to Use in the Agentic Era, One Useful Thing, 18 February 2026, first paragraph

question.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four principles in Mollick's Co-Intelligence?
options: Always invite AI to the table
Be the human in the loop
Assume this is the worst AI you will ever use
question.explain: The four principles are: always invite AI to the table, be the human in the loop, treat AI like a person (but tell it what kind of person it is), and assume this is the worst AI you will ever use. Data rules are real, but they come from your institution, not from the book. At the Bank, internal documents go to Copilot, not to public chatbots.

days.do: Do what the guide says: take one document you actually need today, give your AI a hard task on it, and push back twice on the answer. If you are at the Bank and the document is internal, that means Copilot. Then come back to Five Mornings and build your own course from it.
